Additionally, a liquid hydrogen tanker truck costs around $1–$2 million, and a gaseous tube trailer truck is roughly $1 million as of 2025 (Argonne National Laboratory n.d.; Munster 2025). Liquid-hydrogen-carrying trucks typically have storage tanks with a double-wall stainless steel design where the space between the inner and outer shell is vacuum insulated to minimize heat 51 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. transfer by conduction and convection. To reduce heat transfer via radiation, reflective material is typically layered in the vacuum space (Wijnans and Cardella, n.d.). Chart Industries and Linde are two companies that have commercially developed liquid hydrogen tanker truck technology (Linde 2025; Chart Industries, n.d.-b). If airport LH demand exceeds about 10 MTPD, three or more liquid hydrogen tanker truck 2 deliveries would be needed each day. The logistics of liquid hydrogen truck delivery are more difficult at this point, especially because a single delivery truck may take up to 4 hours to unload (from arrival to departure including all necessary safety checks and procedures) with conventional pressure-based transfers, and space constraints might make it impossible to unload multiple truckloads at a time (Argonne National Laboratory n.d.). Multiple truck deliveries per day would also increase traffic congestion to and from the airport. At airport demand levels greater than 10 MTPD, cryogenic supply options such as on-site production and liquefaction or pipeline delivery and on-site liquefaction become more economically viable. As of 2025, more than 1,600 miles of gaseous hydrogen pipeline are in operation in the United States. These pipelines connect large hydrogen supply with industrial demand nodes and are concentrated in the Gulf Coast of the United States (DOE n.d.-a). For comparison, the natural gas network in the United States consists of about 3 million miles of transmission, distribution, and gathering pipelines in total (Figure 34) (EIA 2024b). For LH -powered aircraft at airports, 2 gaseous hydrogen pipelines would be a suitable delivery option to explore as LH demand scales. 2 A hydrogen pipeline could connect a central production facility or an underground salt cavern used for gaseous hydrogen storage directly to the airport. However, space constraints at an airport must be considered with this approach, as a liquefaction plant would be needed at the pipeline outlet to meet aircraft LH demands. 2 52 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications.
